pages.title: Read the situation
pages.instruction: The course brief. Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Learner profile · simulated source
pages.subject: A practical project, not a certificate alone
paragraphs: The fictional learner wants feedback on a practical project. They can usually attend Wednesday evenings and a Friday check-in, while Tuesday is a fixed commitment. The lower fee is attractive, but they are willing to consider a higher cost if the learning can be applied directly. Finishing sooner would help, although it is not a firm deadline.

Two details remain uncertain: whether the timetable could change, and how closely feedback relates to the learner’s project. A recommendation should name those uncertainties. The learner has not said that flexibility outweighs every other criterion, and the two course formats should not be reduced to cheap versus good.

pages.title: Read the situation
pages.instruction: The comparable options. Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Course comparison · simulated source
pages.subject: Cost, schedule and application
paragraphs: Course A costs $180 for eight weeks. It currently lists Wednesday sessions from seven to nine, practical tasks and feedback during class. Course B costs $320 for twelve weeks. It lists independent work, a Friday six o’clock check-in and a project discussed at that check-in. These are simulated offers for decision practice.

The comparison does not establish which teaching is better or guarantee an outcome. The key question is how each format meets the learner’s actual needs. A more expensive option may be feasible without being automatically preferable. Ask what information could change the balance before turning a tentative recommendation into an unconditional one.

pages.title: Listen and answer
pages.instruction: A preference becomes a constraint. Listen for the new information and decide how to respond
pages.message: Hi, Ana. Course A has changed its live session from Wednesday to Tuesday, still seven to nine. The person on our brief has a regular Tuesday commitment and cannot attend live then. The provider also says the practical feedback is only given during that live class, not on a recording afterwards. The price and eight-week length are unchanged. This turns attendance from a flexible preference into a serious constraint. Course B’s Friday check-in still fits, but we should confirm whether its feedback covers the person’s project before accepting the higher cost. Could you explain how the balance has changed rather than simply saying the more expensive course is now better? There may also be a later run of A worth asking about
